utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, would you have the witness brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters and to the court reporters, who always work with a great deal of competence. Good morning to counsel, both Defence and Prosecution. Good morning to the accused, who is our witness. I'm saying this for the public gallery. The people in the public gallery don't know the proceedings as well as we do. This is the part of the Blaskic trial, and the accused is acting as a witness. He's under oath. The Trial Chamber is considering him to be a witness now. Mr. Nobilo, we can continue now. The morning will be long, but according to logical sequences, we can take our breaks, which will allow the accused or the witness to rest as he needs. We will try to take a break around 10.00, but according to what you consider to be the most appropriate. All right. Mr. Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we ended yesterday with the description of the events of the 24th of April, 1993. So let us go on to the next day and days to see what happened of significance from the standpoint of this trial, rather than from the standpoint of the war.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 25th of April already, about 7.50, there was strong tank shelling by BH army forces of Busovaca, and at 8.00, there was strong attack against the territory under the defence of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca. We tried to send reinforcements, that is, some 20 men, and sometime in the afternoon, we managed to actually send them there. I had a rather brief meeting with Mr. de la Mota towards evening, about 19.00 on the 25th of April, and the immediate cause for the meeting was an incident and tensions that were running high between the inhabitants and soldiers of the village of Divjak and members of the UNPROFOR base at Divjak. The reason for this incident, as I was informed by Mr. de la Mota, was that the soldiers had asked UNPROFOR to participate in pulling out the bodies of the killed relatives from the village of Divjak. There were two civilians -- the bodies of two civilians and of three HVO soldiers that UNPROFOR's assistance was requested for. There were no other consequences, except for tension between UNPROFOR and the village of Divjak. I also tried at the time to put in order the data from the front, though the front was some 80 kilometres long in Travnik and Novi Travnik --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the front towards the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is this front (indicating). In Busovaca, the front was about 38 kilometres long, and in Vitez about 28 kilometres long. That was the total width of the front. So that a large number of personnel, conscripts, and able-bodied men were engaged on those front lines. On the 26th of April, I had a meeting with Mr. Nakic, who was a member of the joint command, and at the morning meeting, he informed me about the activities of the joint command designed to set up a joint command in Travnik. Then we also spoke about the road corridors, about the removal of snipers from certain positions. I initiated this discussion, asking him to discuss it with Mr. Dzemo Merdan, to ask him to have sniper groups removed from the positions of Grbavica, Sljibcica, and Barin Gaj. We also pointed out that we also have to raise at the joint command the problem of water supply, namely, the tanks for supplying Vitez and Zenica were under the control of the BH army, and there was a shortage of water already in the town of Vitez and the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about the shortage of water, was this due to natural causes or was it because the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Kruscica had closed off the water supply or temporarily, at least?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The water tanks were under the control of the BH army, and I checked with the mayor of Vitez, and his position and mine was that the army had closed off the water flow, so that later on, Vitez would be left without water for some time. Due to the low pressure of the system, Zenica was short of water as well. It will be evident from the later event that I frequently raised this matter with representatives of the UNHCR and the Red Cross, asking them to mediate so that the water supply could be restored to normal. I also asked Nakic to raise the issue of the separation of forces, that is, for UNPROFOR to begin to patrol the route from Vrhovine via Kratine, Jelinak, and Putis, so that the first stage of separation of forces could begin and security ensured for future activities, in the first place, for conducting the investigation. In the course of the day, I received information from the military intelligence, and it actually came from the 111th Special Purpose Brigade in Zepce, and they reported that they had intercepted a conversation between the BH army -- among the BH army forces, saying that they would not give up their concept and that two nations or peoples could not live in the same area, that is, the faithful and the infidels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 111th Brigade is not a special purpose brigade but an XP brigade.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not a special purpose brigade. It is a home guard's brigade. They said that the faithful and infidels could not live in the same territory, and that the key to everything was the explosives factory in Vitez, and the idea would be to have a black flag with Arabic inscriptions. In the night between the 25th and the 26th, I called up Dzemo again because of the information I had received that the 91st Anti-Sabotage Detachment of the BH army was opening fire on HVO positions, and I required that he too intervene and put an end to these provocations. As I was unable to reach him, I decided, with the help of Nakic and other associates in the joint command, to send a message to Travnik, to Dzemo, saying that I was looking for him and that we were having problems because of these provocations by the Anti-Sabotage Detachment of the BH army. When my associate told Dzemo that we had been calling him all night, Dzemo's answer to my associate was the following: "You called me last night five times, and I have been running around after you for a whole year. The Mujahedeen will cost you your lives. It is our time now." On the 26th, in the afternoon, I received information from members of the joint command in Travnik that the commander of the 306th Brigade in Han Bila, the 306th Brigade of the BH army, commenting on the peace agreement signed on the 21st of April in Vitez had stated: "Whoever signed an agreement on the separation of forces is a fool," the separation of forces between the BH army and the HVO. After the officers of the joint command told him that it had been signed by two commanders, Halilovic and Petkovic, his comment was that Halilovic probably didn't know what he was signing or didn't see what he was signing. On the 27th of April, in the morning, there was a mist still. I went by the road that we managed to make between the 23rd and the 27th to the village of Ahmici, and I toured a part of the village. I saw burned houses in the village, and there was still some embers. They may have been burned during the night or set fire to. I saw the minaret and mosque and other signs of destruction. I held a press conference in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us stop just for a moment. When you reached Ahmici, you said that it was misty. Did you have an armoured vehicle or did you use an ordinary vehicle and risk it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had a regular vehicle. I never had an armoured vehicle, and we had only just managed to lay this road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After seeing what had happened to Ahmici, for the first time, you went to hold a press conference in Busovaca. Will you explain to the Trial Chamber, was this a regular press conference, an extraordinary press conference, and what was the purpose of those press conferences that you held, and who were those present?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These conferences were our regular communication with the public of the Lasva River Valley, because under conditions of a blockade of the media, that was the only way, by word of mouth, for us to address both conscripts and civilians, and all the inhabitants of this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you address the people present? What medium did you use?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mostly these press conferences were recorded on VHS videotape, and then these would be broadcast where possible. These press conferences were carried live, but I think this was only possible much later in Busovaca. In most cases, they were recorded, and then immediately after the completion of the recording, they would be distributed to municipal studios which would broadcast them during the next few days and weeks because that was the only way to communicate with the entire population. They were very popular. They were open to the public, and almost always, they were attended by somebody from the UN or humanitarian organisations. They would be present with their interpreters so they could follow the proceedings directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, in Busovaca municipality and in Vitez municipality, did the municipal authorities organise some small local TV stations that could broadcast these tapes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were, in Busovaca and Vitez municipalities, local municipal TV stations which rebroadcast these press conferences. There was a local TV station in Kiseljak as well, but after the corridor between Kiseljak and Busovaca was cut, they could not take over these tapes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any important newspapers, or was the main purpose of those press conferences to address the people via the medium of television?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were no daily newspapers, except if a local unit, at the level of a company or battalion, managed to issue some kind of journal of its own, but there were no regular daily newspapers. As far as I know, there were no publications published in that area. This was the only way for us to inform the people there of what was happening, and I know that there was a great demand for information because there were very few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, in the course of the day, and after the press conference, and on the day of the press conference, how frequently, on the average, would the recording of that press conference be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the day of the press conference itself, at least three or four times or every subsequent hour. Also on the following days until the next press conference, because, in fact, there was no other programme except for local cameramen to try and make some video recordings locally, and to try to show those recordings on the television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that press conference, what is it that you needed to tell the HVO army and the people of the Lasva Valley? Try to remember exactly, and to choose your words in telling Their Honours about this.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I came to the press conference from the village of Ahmici, and I, roughly, said the following: That I was horrified, and that I condemned the crime committed in the village of Ahmici, that it was the duty of the joint commission to conduct an investigation because I still believed that the joint commission would devote its intention to this matter, with the help of international representatives. I said whoever committed it, committed an organised, systematic, and planned crime, and I'm sure that it was conducted under somebody's control. I also said that those responsible for the crime must be identified and must be called to task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go on to analyse your words, was the British journalist from the BBC present at that press conference?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Martin Bell from the BBC. I'm not sure whether other journalists were present, but I think representatives from the Belgium and the Dutch battalions were there. I'm not sure. I don't know their names. They had a base there, and they almost regularly attended our press conferences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you need to say to the army and the people that you were horrified by the crime in Ahmici? From this time distance, how would you explain it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were two issues that were ever present in my mind at the time. One was to make it clear that this was a major tragedy that should never be repeated. Secondly, I also wanted to make it clear that the investigation would seek to identify and discover the perpetrators. Addressing the people, most of whom I believed were decent people, I wanted their assistance in initiating and conducting the investigation. This was an issue that people didn't like to talk about, even later, and then in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said immediately it is a crime. Does that mean that you couldn't accept the interpretation that such devastation could be the result of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did not accept that that could be the consequence of fighting in inhabited areas because I saw that the damage was widespread and considerable. Fighting in inhabited areas certainly is accompanied by the risk of collateral damage and casualties, but as far as I have been able to study, very few commanders opt for fighting in inhabited areas because it is very difficult to envisage the reaction and behaviour of soldiers in well-structured armies even. However, this devastation was vast in every respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time on TV cameras and addressing the entire population of the Lasva Valley, you said that the crime had been committed in an organised manner, systematically, on the basis of a plan, and under somebody's control or command. Could you explain those four points of your allegations? Why did you say that, first, that it was an organised systematic, planned and controlled operation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, it could not have been done by a group of three or four drunken persons, drunken soldiers, and that they had done it of their own accord. When I said that it was organised, I felt that there must have been some preparation behind it, preparation for such destruction. When I said that it was done on a planned basis, if a single group would act arbitrarily, then certainly every single house along the road up to the mosque would not have been burnt. Also, it was never clear to me why a religious facility had been destroyed, and when I say that it was under somebody's control, it means that I was sure that the group that committed it was under the control of an elected commander of its own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that this was done in a planned manner and under someone's control, do you make this conclusion on the basis of the type of operation and the consequences of that operation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Judging by the scope of the destruction, because there was fighting on the 16th in 22 different locations. There were conflicts in January 1993, but the intensity of destruction was not accompanied by such destruction of facilities, as was the case here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time or later, did you manage to learn who had planned and organised and controlled this operation? Did you ever manage to find that out? Were you informed of it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I never got the names nor any kind of reports as to who was the perpetrator, who was the organiser, or who had planned the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo. Were you, General, able to make an assessment of the time period during which the destruction was undertaken? How much time do you think was needed for what was done?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, I thought it was about one or two days, that is to say, all of the 16th possibly, but it was very difficult to make any kind of assessment because it was my very first time to see such destruction too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What was the size of force which you think was required?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm going to give you my assessment, Your Honour, from 20 to 40 men, 50 at maximum, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you were at the press conference, you told the Honourable Judge that one or two days were needed. Tell me, after having heard all the witness and victims here in this courtroom, what do you think? How much time did it take for this crime to be committed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I recall, from about 05.25, 05.30 up to 07.30, 08.00 at maximum, having listened to the statements of the victims of this crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you know this fact, does it increase or decrease your conviction that this was an organised crime, that it was carried out systematically and according to a plan?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This only intensifies my conviction that it was so because the time period during which this destruction took place was very short. During two or two and a half hours, everything began and ended, that is to say, that it had to be an organised activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, are you the first one in the Lasva Valley to call what happened in the Lasva Valley and Ahmici a crime, in public at that time, not in a private conversation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you're referring to HVO officers, yes, I believe I was the first, but it seems to me that Colonel Stewart sent that letter, and in the letter it said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was not precise. I'm talking about the Croatian side. Did anybody define that which happened in Ahmici as a crime before you did?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, as I say, publicly, in the media, and perhaps we can even say until the present day, did anyone on the Croatian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina define Ahmici as a crime, publicly in the media, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not remember anyone having defined it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, in a press conference, questions are asked. You speak about that press conference as a kind of a statement that you would make. There were journalists, I suppose, from the entire world or from the main organisations of the media. What questions did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, at that time, this was a theatre of war and there were not journalists from all over the world. I remember that the BBC team was there, and I recall a journalist or an officer from the Belgian or Dutch battalion, and there were local journalists. The questions that were put at that time were aimed at the problems of investigation and survival and further developments in the war. As regards foreign journalists, there weren't any, only the BBC team and perhaps Sky news. At some point they were there, but whether it was that point, I don't know. I can't say for sure whether the Sky news team was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked about what had happened in Ahmici and what your opinion was about that, or did you say it on your own?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no one asked me about it. Nobody asked me about Ahmici. Questions that were put were primarily aimed at the front, the situation in the Lasva River Valley, the lack of observance in the cease-fire, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the first to speak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you open the press conference with that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I started the press conference with that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did any of the local journalists ask you about this in greater detail or did they all keep quiet about it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that they all shared the initial shock with me, and no questions were put in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were there many of you there? Were there officers from your staff, from your headquarters, or were you alone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had two escorts with me and my driver. Officers did not come with me because there were very few of us anyway, and at the time, they were involved in the joint command, and others were involved in other affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were there still some villages there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In the part where we were, there was livestock that was killed, and there wasn't anyone. Also, there were the remains of burned houses and things. If you're asking about the village of Ahmici, when I visited --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, the question itself, was it related to the press conference or to the village? Was there anyone in the village or was there anyone at the press conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No. I was asking whether General Blaskic, in the villages that had been destroyed, whether there were still any people there? Were there old people there or people who wanted to leave? Was the village completely deserted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The village was completely deserted when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you go into some of the houses?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I passed by the houses, perhaps two or three metres away, but I didn't enter any houses, but I passed by houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are going to finish with this. Now, let us proceed with the course of that particular day. A new agreement seems to have been signed between President Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, at 15.30, I received information that a new agreement had been signed between President Izetbegovic and Boban, but I did not receive any additional information as to what kind of agreement this was, nor was I aware of the contents of the agreement. I also received information on the regrouping of forces of the 7th Muslim Brigade in front of the villages of Krcevine and Jardol, to the north of Vitez. On that day, for the first time, I received information from Nakic, the chief of staff, that a total of 12 Croats were imprisoned and that they were alive within the 7th Muslim Brigade. Nine of them were members of the HVO and three Croats were journalists of Radio Zenica. During the course of the day, I sent a request to the International Red Cross to visit these prisoners, these 12 prisoners that were held by the 7th Muslim Brigade, and to submit information to us on the condition that they were in. The answers received until then by the International Red Cross were to the effect that they had no possibility to check on the prisoners that were under the control of the 7th Muslim Brigade or to visit them or, rather, that the 7th Muslim Brigade did not allow the International Red Cross to monitor the condition of prisoners at all. On that day, there was this capturing from both sides, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik. So it would happen that during the course of the day, one person would be captured several times, brought into custody, and released. There were problems again in terms of moving between Zenica and Vitez. I spoke of that earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us stop at this point. What is the point of this capturing? Why did Muslims capture Croats and Croats capture Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The purpose was to get housing facilities most often or to have private exchanges, but the most frequent motive was to resolve existential problems in a new area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to put a question to you that pertains to you personally. I believe that we have seen that quite a few Muslims had left the territory of Vitez. They left their houses, their apartments. Many people with weapons tried to move in. Could you explain to the Court, where did you live with your wife throughout the war in the Lasva River Valley? Did you ever get an apartment? Did you ever get a house?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask for an apartment or a house. I had an office and I had a screen, and we used part of this space behind the screen as living quarters, and my office was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you lived in your headquarters, slept there and worked there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In Kiseljak, it was in the barracks, and at Vitez, at headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is to say, in the Hotel Vitez, at your headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps one more question. At the very beginning of 1992, the municipal authorities of Kiseljak gave you an apartment. Did you take it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never used that apartment that was allocated to me, and it is true that an apartment was allocated to me, but I never spent any time there, not even an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were commander of an army, regardless of the way this army was established and the extent to which this army was established. Why didn't you get an decent house for yourself or an apartment? Did you think about this? What were your motives?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In a situation when every military conscript was somewhere on the front line, I didn't think that I needed a more comfortable dwelling, and I usually lived, worked, and slept at headquarters. It is true that an apartment was allocated to me by the municipal authorities in Kiseljak, and it was empty for a certain period of time, but I thought it was not moral for me to use this apartment, knowing that most of the families of the persons who were killed were not taken care of properly, that there were many exiled persons, that there were many wounded, that there were many refugees from other sides where people had suffered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us skip the chronological order. At the time moment when you heard about this indictment on the radio, you were a chief of staff of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a very high position. Tell the Court, where were you at that time when you heard about the indictment? Did you have a villa at your disposal, as most generals did?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most generals did, but I did not. I don't regret it. I lived in Citluk, in a ground-floor building that used to be a garage. I lived with Danko Dugandzic. It was his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that didn't belong to you either?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that was not mine, never. It was just rented out during the time that I was chief of staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please proceed with the chronological order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 28th of April, I received information around 04.20 about a strong attack against Gradina launched by the BH army. It is to the south of Kuber, practically the last point behind the Zenica-Busovaca and the Zenica-Vitez roads. At 07.40, I received information that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had taken Gradina and repelled the HVO forces and, in that way, brought the position of Kaonik itself under fire and control, that is to say, they had under their control most of the main road between Vitez and Zenica. The members of the joint commission, including Nakic and the other officers, before they set out to Travnik for a meeting, were also informed about this attack, and I asked for this question to be raised once again because it was obvious that in the early morning hours, new conquests were being made and that they were improving their already good tactical positions, that is to say, the army vis-à-vis the HVO. After that, I received information that the military police had looted the house of Vlado Baskarad from Vitez. Vlado Baskarad was a Croat. He had a shop of his own. I asked for the equipment and everything else that was looted to be returned to the owner, and I was surprised when I realised that his goods were actually taken away from him and that he was given a receipt about that. So I thought that this was some kind of mobilisation that was unlawful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of goods was this; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember it was alcohol and some other goods, but I do remember alcohol, and that must have been the motive. A certificate had been given as if mobilisation had been carried out. Then I also received information that the members of the broken-up Zenica units of the HVO were arriving through forests, either individually or in groups, in the territory of the municipality of Travnik, that is to say, Grahovcici, Brajkovici, and the area of the Vitez municipality as they were crossing the front lines. Some of them arrived unharmed, whereas others were wounded as they passed through that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time, how many refugees, how many new refugees, did you already have?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, at that time, my assessment is that there was between 3.000 and 5.000 refugees from Zenica in the area of the Lasva River Valley. Then around 13.50, I had a meeting with the mayor of Vitez, Mr. Santic, who conveyed to me the conversation or, rather, the content of conversation he had with the Vice-President of the municipal assembly of Zenica, Mr. Dominik Sakic. Dominik Sakic, at the same time, was the president of the HVO for Zenica, and Sakic informed him about the situation that prevailed at the time in Zenica, about the abduction of Commander Totic having been planned, and also about the disarmament of the HVO of Zenica by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then in Zenica, about 24 civilians, Croat civilians, had been killed. Out of them, a little girl had been killed, and a Croat had his throat slit. Then also that the wounded could not receive visits by the Red Cross or by priests in hospitals, and that in the penitentiary there were about 450 Croat prisoners, that is to say, military conscripts, and civilians at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Zivko Totic and those four officers who were abducted before the war, were they still in prison? Did you manage to reach them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did not manage to reach them, but fortunately, on the 27th of April, we received this information that it was certain that 12 Croats were held by the 7th Muslim Brigade, and we asked the Red Cross to see them, to see the conditions that they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps we could stop at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you prefer to stop now. Is that because you're going to move into another sequence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness be shown document D365?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 27th of April, '93, you are issuing an order to the Vitez saying: "Supplement to the order of 24 April, '93, number 01-4-560, and the order itself says: 1. I prohibit any treatment of temporarily detained civilians which is contrary to the basic provisions of the Geneva Convention. 2. This order comes into effect immediately, and the brigade commander is responsible to me for its execution." Tell us, please, did you issue that order? If you did, what were the reasons and what were your concerns?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did issue this order and draft it. A moment ago, before the break actually, I said that about 5.000 exiles or, rather, between 3.000 and 5.000 exiles were arriving from Zenica and that there were some rather emotional reactions and even revenge among those refugees who were coming with their equipment and weapons, and they were, by force, breaking into apartments, capturing Bosniak Muslim civilians, persecuting them, and engaging in various other unlawful acts. I wish to underline once again, through this order to the commander of the Vitez Brigade, that the treatment of civilians has to be in accordance with the regulations in effect, that is, free of any violence or any other adverse behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go on. We were talking about the 28th of April when you mentioned your meeting with Santic, who conveyed to you information about his conversation with Sakic in Zenica about the condition of Croats in Zenica. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that meeting, the town mayor of Vitez told me that the Croats in Zenica were out of their minds with fear, that they were fleeing Zenica in the direction of Zepce, Novi Seher. Some were fleeing towards Kakanj. The majority of Croats were fleeing to Vitez and Busovaca. He also told me that Croatian flats were being broken into by night in Zenica by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and that they were taking away Croatian men of military age for interrogation during the night, and then they would bring them back usually in the mornings. These interrogations were accompanied by physical mistreatment in most cases. Also that most of the able-bodied men in Zenica were not sleeping in their homes, fearing such abductions. They were hiding during the night in the woods or in some neighbouring settlements outside of town. He also told me that what caused the greatest fear was the prison of the 7th Muslim Brigade, in the music school in Zenica, also that every checkpoint held by the BH army had a list of able-bodied Croats from Zenica, and that at those checkpoints, Croats were being taken prisoner once they were identified on the list, regardless of whether they were members of the HVO or not. The sole criterion was their ethnicity. Mayor Santic told me that Sakic's message from Zenica was that we should inform the International Red Cross about all this, as well as the European Monitoring Mission, and that we should ask for assistance for the Croats in Zenica. In the course of the day, in the command, we addressed the problem of evacuating the wounded from the hospital because there wasn't enough room in the hospital. So we put up the wounded in the neighbouring private houses next to the hospital. In the course of the day, I tasked my associates to check the implementation of the signed agreement with the BH army and to continue with the structuring and formation of the Vitez Brigade. It was already evident at the time, regarding military operations in the Lasva Valley, that there was combat from 02.00 to 07.00 carried out by members of the BH army, and as a result of that fighting, they captured better positions while concealing their activities by carrying them out in the early morning hours. In the course of the day, I again requested that my associates supply me with better quality, more comprehensive and more accurate reports because the tendency continued of reports on combat operations arriving upon the completion of those same operations. This prevented me from providing proper control and command in real time. In the course of the day, the mayor of Vitez, Santic, came to me rather worried and conveyed a part of the conversation that he had had with Colonel Stewart, the commander of the British Battalion of UNPROFOR. Santic told me that at the meeting with Santic, Stewart had said the following, and I quote: "You, the HVO, are on the brink of military defeat, and you are in a far worse position than the forces of the BH army. Second, identify the perpetrators of Ahmici because the BH army will certainly come and react or, rather, take revenge for all the victims of Ahmici." After this conversation with Mayor Santic, sometime after 20.00, about 20.30, in fact, I was called up by phone and told to get ready, that I had to attend a meeting in Zenica. The call was from General Petkovic, who was Brigadier at the time, the chief of staff of the HVO, who informed me that UNPROFOR would provide transportation from Vitez to Zenica where I had to attend a meeting. At about 21.30, I attended a meeting between representatives of the BH army and representatives of the HVO. Representing the BH army were the chief of the main staff of the BH army, General Sefer Halilovic; also the deputy chief of staff of the BH army, Mr. Stjepan Siber; a member of the main staff of the BH army, Mr. Vehbija Karic; the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army, Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic; and also present was Mr. Rasim Delic. I'm not sure whether he attended in the capacity of commander of the main logistics centre of the BH army staff from Visoko or in some other capacity because I know that before April '93, he was the commander of the main logistics centre in Visoko. The HVO was represented by Brigadier Petkovic, the chief of the main staff of the Croatian Defence Council, Officer Andric, and myself. As the meeting started as soon as I arrived, I just managed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Who chaired the meeting? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by the head of the European Monitoring Mission, Mr. Thebault, but, Mr. President, I am not sure whether anyone accompanied him. I know that Mr. Thebault was there for sure. Before the beginning of the meeting, I managed to brief Brigadier Petkovic on the current military situation, telling him that we had lost the position Gradina above Kaonik on the main Busovaca-Zenica road, and after that, the meeting started. In the course of the meeting, Brigadier Petkovic was given the floor and he said the following: "The separation of forces of the army and the HVO has not been carried out, and attacks by the BH army are continuing against the HVO of Busovaca and the HVO of Vitez." After that, Sefer Halilovic said: "The truce is not being observed, and let us resolve the problem of the cease-fire and let us then begin to discuss everything else." Brigadier Petkovic responded by saying, "Halilovic, you did not issue the order in Konjic or Jablanica or in Busovaca or Vitez, and you see what is happening. The fighting is continuing. Order a cease-fire and stop these attacks or I will go back to Mostar from here. If your units have received orders to move forward, to advance, then they can also be given orders to retreat." This is what Brigadier Petkovic told Halilovic. Halilovic then asked his 3rd Corps commander, "Dzedo, what are your reports?" The 3rd Corps commander, whose nickname was Dzedo, and his real name was Enver Hadzihasanovic, replied, "I was in the field all day, and I haven't yet studied all the reports." After some discussion, conclusions were adopted at this meeting of the following content: 1. To immediately order a cease-fire. Then the next day, tomorrow, at 09.00, have another meeting in the same composition and work on the implementation of the cease-fire order on the ground. The location of the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be in Zenica and in Mostar, and the joint command will be composed of the chiefs of staff of the BH army and of the main staff of the HVO with their associates. The joint command of the 3rd Corps and of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia will be designated at the next meeting, that is, the position or the location of that joint command. When the meeting ended, I returned the same way I had come, that is, in UNPROFOR vehicles, from Zenica to Vitez. On the next day, that is, the 29th of April, 1993, at 09.30, we had a meeting in Vitez. The meeting was chaired by Mr. Thebault, and the BH army delegation was composed again of the chief of staff of the main staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic; his deputy Mr. Stjepan Siber; deputy Mr. Vehbija Karic; and Mr. Rasim Delic. The commander of the 3rd Corps did not come to the meeting in Vitez. On behalf of the HVO, there was the chief of staff of the HVO, Brigadier Petkovic; Officer Andric; Commander Filipovic; I was there; and the chief of staff, Mr. Franjo Nakic. The agenda of that meeting was as follows: First, the work of the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then the situation in the territory of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. It was agreed at that meeting that the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be based in Zenica, in the building of the theatre or the municipality, and that two weeks later it would move to Mostar. The idea was that this joint command would operate for two weeks of the month in Zenica and the other two weeks in Mostar. The main function of the joint command was planning and execution of a joint struggle against the army of Republika Srpska. For the base of the joint command of the 3rd Corps and the operational Zone of Central Bosnia, the town of Travnik was chosen. Point 2, that is, the situation on the ground: There was also a discussion on the fighting on the front lines of the Busovaca front, and this fighting was most intensive at Kula. When the meeting ended in the second half of the day, I received a message from the head of the Military Intelligence Service who had recorded a conversation between the commander of the 306th Brigade of the BH army and the commander of the 325th Brigade of the BH army, in which they said the following: "We'll see one another at the bus station in Vitez. We will link up at Lasva."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lasva is the river flowing through Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, through Vitez along the main road. "Everyone has not done everything they should. Now we have to work harder, and we must not relax but must use all means at our disposal."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we stop there for a moment and make an analysis of the military situation? If the Lasva River flows through the middle of the valley, where would the army forces come from to link up at the Lasva River? Could you show that to us?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The conversation between the commander of the -- well, the 325th Brigade had most of its forces here in Kruscica (indicating), and the command post of the 306th Brigade is in Han Bila, and this road leads to the main road between Vitez and Travnik, and it was mostly under the control of the 306th Brigade. The Lasva River, I'm showing it right now (indicating), passes along the main road through the valley and canyon to Kaonik and further on to the Bosna River. This conversation in which it was said, "See you at the bus station," the bus station is about 30 to 50 metres away from the Vitez Hotel where my headquarters was. The Lasva River is nearby too. If linking up at the Lasva Valley was the message, that meant in this area between Vitez, Divjak, via Gradina and Kruscica. It is this direction (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, on that day, that is, the 28th of April, 1993, what were the closest positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? In other words, how many metres did they need for this link-up?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Their closest position was 50 metres away from the main road, that is, Dzidica Kuce and the forces from Kruscica. The maximum distance is 1.000 to 1.500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say, the northern and the southern forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were 1.500 metres away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but the position of Divjak, Grbavica, and then a few hundred metres, and then Stari Vitez, all of that was completely linked up, and also the bridge on the Lasva Valley was also under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Stari Vitez and the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Divjak, that was uninterrupted BH army-held territory. What was the distance?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: About 500 to 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We can go back now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: D366, please, could we see that now? Could it please be given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like a clarification, Mr. Blaskic. There were two meetings on the 28th and the 29th of April, one in Zenica and one in Vitez. Was there never any question at all about Ahmici, not by Thebault or the Bosnian side or yourself, in fact, you who had held a press conference? It seemed to be a major problem for Colonel Stewart, but really nobody spoke about Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my notes, I do not have anything written down about anybody's mention of Ahmici. Had anyone mentioned Ahmici, I imagine I would have written this down. However, Mr. President, I was brought to this meeting and it started practically as soon as I walked into the room. I wrote down the agenda. After that, on the 30th of April, in the afternoon hours, after 16.40, Ahmici was discussed at yet another meeting that I shall be speaking of, but this is the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to take this moment to ask the following question: General Blaskic said that before the beginning of the meeting, you had informed Petkovic about the situation, that is, the military situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the moment as I was taking my seat by him, and it only took a few minutes in the sense of what the situation was and what the problems were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Did you speak about Ahmici with Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the meeting, I could not, and I did (sic), but I did speak about it on the 30th of April to Brigadier Petkovic because he was being driven by the members of the Spanish Battalion according to a special arrangement, so we were not together, except for the duration of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, at the meeting, was Petkovic already informed about what had happened in Ahmici or was he not informed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the meeting, he wasn't, but he was informed about it previously, that is to say, he was informed of the content of my talk with Colonel Stewart. Everything that happened on the 24th, I sent all of this in writing to the Brigadier, and he was informed about all activities as of the 24th of April, but not at the meeting, but earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have document D366, which is actually your order from the 29th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to interrupt for a moment. I wonder if there isn't a difference between the English and French interpretation in respect of General Blaskic's answer to the question as to whether or not he had spoken with General Petkovic about Ahmici or whether General Petkovic had been informed about Ahmici. On the current page of the transcript, on at 17 of page 38. In the English text, it says that there was a discussion with Colonel Stewart, whereas in French I heard about a conversation with General Petkovic. Perhaps we could reconcile this or go back to the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, you heard what Mr. Fourmy said. So it was with General Petkovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I did not discuss Ahmici at that meeting with General Petkovic because I was brought in just before the meeting started. I was not in a position to discuss this subject. But I also said that earlier he had been informed about these events, including the content of my meeting with Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say, that earlier on, you informed Petkovic about the content of your conversation with Colonel Stewart; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: More specifically, I believe General Blaskic said that you had already informed Petkovic on the 24th of April; is that correct? Did I hear correctly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will try to read the order D366 of the 29th of April, 1993. The copy is not a very good one, at least not in the Croat original, but I think that we will be able to read the key sentences. So I'm reading the order: "On the basis of the joint order of the chief of HVO main headquarters and the chief of the main staff of the BH army of the 29th of April, 1993, in order to carry it out, I hereby order: 1. Immediately draft lists of detained civilians (men, women, children) including the following information: a) personal information (day, month, year, and place of birth); b) address of residence and signature of the person concerned. RESPONSIBLE: Immediate subordinate commanders. DEADLINE: 30 April, 1993, 10.00. 2. Release all civilians (men, women, children) arrested during the conflicts between the BH army and the HVO. RESPONSIBLE: Immediate subordinate commanders. DEADLINE: 30 April, 1993, 12.00. 3. Joint operative teams shall establish contact and immediately commence clearing the battlefield, i.e., the collection of the dead and their burial. There shall be no combat activities or provocation during the collection of bodies. The families of the dead shall be notified of the names of the dead and the place where the bodies were collected. RESPONSIBLE: Immediate subordinate commanders in respective zones of responsibility. DEADLINE: 30 April, 1993, 16.00. 4. All released civilians must be guaranteed full safety in the locations in your zones of responsibility, and you shall be held responsible for the situation," unfortunately, the rest is illegible. "5. Immediate subordinate commanders and brigade commanders shall be responsible for the full execution of this order by 10.00 on 1 May, 1993. They must submit a written report with lists containing the following information: a) the name of released civilians; b) the names of those killed (should there be no changes, copy the data from the previous report); c) names of those buried. 6. In carrying out this order, cooperate with UNPROFOR, ICRC, UNHCR, and EU representatives. Signed, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, Commander." Tell me, first of all, to the best of your knowledge, in Vitez or in Busovaca, in the enclave that was under your command after the conflict broke out, were there any imprisoned civilians, women and children?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were. There were civilians who were taken prisoner. There were also private imprisonment. People were taken into custody according to private arrangements. This order was made so that this problem could be resolved according to the standards of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you comment on point 4 a bit, where you say that your subordinate commanders have to guarantee civilian persons whom they release full security in the locations where they will be released, and they will be held responsible, obviously, for the situation in those locations.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It says here: "And you shall be held responsible for the situation in your zone of responsibility." According to the criteria of the International Red Cross, civilians, prior to their release, had to give their identification data that are sought in the first point, and then they had the right to say where they wanted to live after they were released. That is the question that I spoke of earlier. The civilians could say that they wanted to go to areas that were under BH army control or they could remain in areas under HVO control. In this point, I repeated an action that I already ordered, that is to say, civilians who are released and who state that they wish to remain in the territory of Vitez and in the territory under HVO control, that they must be guaranteed full safety in the zones of responsibility of the brigades. For the Viteska Brigade, it's Vitez. For the Busovaca Brigade, it's Busovaca, and in Novi Travnik, the responsibility of the Novi Travnik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, in terms of the implementation of this order, was there cooperation with the International Red Cross and did the International Red Cross monitor the process of release?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This activity was carried out according to the standards of the International Red Cross both ways, and the International Red Cross did monitor this, and they also set the time for this and everything else. So if it was the standpoint of the International Red Cross that the release could not be carried out, then it was not carried out, that is to say, that the International Red Cross supervised this activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like a clarification in terms of the addressee. You say: "All commanders under my orders," and in parentheses you have "(Brigades and autonomous units, 4th LTRD)." What does that mean "autonomous units that are directly under your orders"? There were units that you recognised as autonomous and then there were those that you said which were under your orders. How can one be both autonomous or independent and under your orders?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, the order states directly in every point who is responsible and when this order is to be carried out, but it is also addressed to immediate subordinates and those who are within the zone of responsibility of Central Bosnia. They should receive it for their information, that is to say, that such and such a person is not responsible for the carrying out of this order but is present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, in this enclave, who was immediately subordinate to you and who was autonomous and who was put at your disposal for certain actions? Could you define these units by name and could you separate them into two categories?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For certain actions, I had the 4th Battalion of the military police and the PPN Vitezovi resubordinated to me, whereas all other units were immediately subordinate to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. But there's perhaps a translation problem. We will go back to this directly and immediately. Perhaps we won't go back to that same discussion we had yesterday about "instantanement" and "immediatement." You're not really explaining what I need to know, General Blaskic. I understood that you always put the names of the people to who this was addressed, but then as Judge Rodrigues called your attention to, the responsible individuals are indicated under each of the points, under each of the points, but when you write "responsible" in the French version, you say, "The commanders direct under my orders," and on the top, we see "Commanders directly under my orders," whereas in parentheses you have that they are autonomous units or independent units. You have complained several times that sometime some of the units didn't obey you. I understand that some the units are dependent, but if you give them the orders and at the same time you say that they are independent, you shouldn't be surprised that they don't obey. How do you justify that? What does that mean, these "independent" units? Was that the military police? Was it the Vitezovi? These are special units, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The units that are not subordinate to me, Mr. President, were the military police and the special purpose units, but here, in every point, I specified who was responsible for carrying out the assignment concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're not making it clear. You're not being specific here, at least in the French version. It's not made specific because you write "Responsible --" let me look under 1. Look under 1. The person responsible, you say, "Commanded directly under my orders." You're not making it very clear, because when you look at the top, you say, "The directors directly under my orders are the brigades or the autonomous units or the 4th, as the LTRD, the Light Artillery Rocket Division, the Motorised Division, the 4th Battalion." There's an entire list. So don't tell me or don't tell us that you made it clear. I'm interested in this because the purpose of this discussion is to hear you frequently say that your orders have not been carried out properly, and I say that perhaps one shouldn't be surprised that they weren't carried out. There were orders, General Blaskic, and that's what you told Judge Rodrigues, and we saw that they were very clearly indicated. They didn't say "Military police," they said, "This unit or that unit," and now you say, "Commanders under my orders." I don't want to add anything further, just to be mentioning that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the structure of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, there were HVO brigades, and there were two units that we called independent units, autonomous units. One was the artillery and the other one was anti-aircraft artillery, but they were in the structure of command of the Operative Zone. They were directly subordinate to me. However, in the structure of the Operative Zone, the 4th Battalion of the military police and the PPN Vitezovi were not directly subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I understand the President to be concerned with a question which is equally concerning me, as to how you understood this order. When you look at the upper right-hand side, do you say that in this order, you were regarding autonomous units as directly under your orders or do you not say so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Units listed here as independent units, the 4th Light Artillery Rocket Division and a mixed battalion are directly under my control, whereas the 4th Military Police Battalion was attached to me for a particular task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I mean, General, is at the particular time when this order was issued on the 29th of April, 1993, were you taking the position that autonomous units, including the 4th Battalion, were directly under your orders?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time this order was written, they were resubordinated to me. At that time, they were resubordinated to me, but they did not become a part of the structure. The structure did not change. They were under my control and command, but the structure of the formation did not change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I have got two questions. I think that we're not going to go back to that discussion that we had yesterday that we all know so well, but I do find that in the English version of your order, we still have the word "immediately" or "immediate." The word "immediately" keeps returning, "all immediate subordinates." However, in the French version, they say "commanders directly under my orders" and "commanders immediately under my orders." They use "immediatement" and "directement." These are different things. I'm not sure whether General Blaskic is trying to make a distinction between "directement," "immediately under my orders," and "immediatement," "immediately under my orders." That's one question. I'll ask both questions together because I think they are related to one another. My second question is the following: You issue an order to all the commanders directly under your orders. Here is my question: Who defined the criterion for issuing the orders? Imagine, General Blaskic, that I say: An order to all the people in this room who are subordinate to me. General Blaskic says, "No, I'm not your subordinate." Perhaps the usher might say, "I'm not your subordinate." Therefore, you are not following my orders. You say, "To all commanders directly under my orders," but perhaps there might be a commander who says "No, I'm not under your orders." "I have a list," you say, "I have criteria and I know," therefore, I take the name, the address, and send the order. Do you understand my question? From the point of view of the execution of the order, you say: "To all my subordinates." However, there might be people who would say, "No, I am not subordinate to you, General Blaskic." Who defined the terms? Let me go back to the two questions. If the distinction between "commander directly under my orders" and "commander immediately under my orders," if there is an operative distinction or not, whether or not that distinction is valid, that's the question, and who defined to whom the order should be directed, that is, all your subordinates? But from the point of view of execution, who gave the definition?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, but this affects the very substance. However, as regards this document, the same word is used in the Croatian original. It's the same case that we had yesterday, but in the French translation, two terms are being used. In the original Croatian, the same word is being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps in this Tribunal we should have a dictionary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We can put it on the ELMO, and you will see the same word. We have highlighted in yellow the word, all three words. They are identical and -- though the question is one that the Defence counsel would like the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I agree that in the French version the words "commander directly under my orders" and "commander immediately under my orders" are two different things, at least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but the Croatian word is the same. Perhaps it would be best to ask the General whether there were different interpretations. The question that you have put, whether there were different interpretations between him and his commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic has to answer this, but I want to point out that it's a very relevant question that's been asked by Judge Rodrigues. Not the same as the one we asked yesterday. Yesterday we noticed that at least in the English and French versions "instantanement" and "immediatement," these two words in French are very close to one other. However, Judge Rodrigues has pointed out correctly, at least as far as my own language is concerned, that "immediatement" and "directement", "immediately" and "directly," are not synonymous. It is General Blaskic who will try to answer the question that our colleague Judge Rodrigues has asked.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I shall try, Your Honours. You asked the question: "Who defined the criteria for this order?" The criteria for this order were interpreted by the two chiefs of staff of the main staff, at the time, commanders of the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, their order said that I should issue an order to brigade commanders and independent units which were directly subordinated to me, that is, within my formation, and I would also issue the order for their information to units that were resubordinated to me, in this case, the 4th Police Battalion which was attached to me on the basis of an order for a particular assignment, whereas later, it goes back to its original structure. Who creates this kind of structure? In the HVO, it was called the administration for organisation attached to the Defence Ministry. They set up the structure of an Operational Zone saying, "It will be such and such. These will be the units within the Operational Zone, and these other units will spend a month in that Operational Zone, and then they will be reassigned to somewhere else. Then they will be linked, some to the defence department and some to the main headquarters." For instance, my chief of staff didn't have a single military police unit, whereas the Defence Minister had several military police battalions. That is how I understood the question. I don't know whether I answered it fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'd like to get into the specifics of the order before we take our break. You issue orders, and we're taking note of the -- look at point 3. How do you apply point 3 to Ahmici? You're talking about clearing out the battlefield and then to collect the dead, that is, to pick up the bodies should not cause any provocations or combat activities. When you issued that order, specifically to the 4th Military Police Battalion, how did you think that that was going to be applied? Didn't you think that there was something a little theoretical in that order? Remember things. You had gone two days earlier to Ahmici. That is an area which is no longer under fire, that you didn't need armoured vehicles to go to Ahmici. Concretely speaking, how could you conceive the collection of dead people in Ahmici? Specifically, how did you --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was an agenda item at the meeting, and that is why reference is made here to joint operative teams, which means Dzemo Merdan and Franjo Nakic will form a joint team consisting of representatives of the HVO holding that front line, in this case, just about Ahmici, and representatives of the BH army who are also controlling the front line above Ahmici, and they would, together with the UNPROFOR forces, go to the site, and with the assistance of the civil defence team, clear the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand that. I reconcile that with your constant or permanent request for investigation. You're going to clear out the battlefield. Each party would pick up its dead, and you think that it would be possible to carry out the investigation, since you are very concerned with the idea of finding those responsible for what happened, you even organised a press conference in order to make sure that these people who committed these crimes be prosecuted and punished. You might even have had some suspicions. Then you set up operational teams. During the meetings of the 29th and the 30th -- the 29th and 30th of April, nobody speaks about Ahmici at those meetings, not even you, and now the bodies are going to be collected, with teams that are going to be working together, joint teams, whereas a few days ago they had massacred one another. This is my question: Don't you think that this is somewhat theoretical, perhaps a bit theoretical? A theoretical document is produced. Do you see it in practical terms, implementation of the document, and perhaps all of this being given to the military police battalion? Don't you find this a bit theoretical?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it was not a theoretical order because the battlefield was, indeed, cleared on that day, not completely, but in Ahmici, among others. I ordered an investigation on the 24th of April, '93, and the security service is conducting the investigation. This was the task of the joint operative centre, and it was certainly in the interests of representatives of the BH army and the HVO for the battlefield to be cleared, and this item was the result of an agreement reached at the meeting on the 29th of April. This was agreed by the two chiefs of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: My point, nobody said that once all the dead had been collected, it had to be done very quickly, of course, but perhaps the investigation, in the end, wouldn't serve much purpose. Nobody said that. Once the battlefield had been cleared out in Ahmici, I suppose that the investigation would have been compromised, severely compromised.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My order for an investigation was not made after this but before, that is, on the 24th of April, my order for an investigation, and this operation was to be done on the 29th of April, which means five days after the order for an investigation was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question in a different way, General Blaskic: If you wanted to have the investigation, as Judge Jorda has just said, that you were very angry about the situation, you had asked for this and that, you organised a press conference, et cetera, and then on that day, with this order, you accepted to have all proof, all remnants of any proof that could have been used for the investigation. All the proof was gone. So if you agree to have the battlefield cleared out, your own priority, in my opinion, if you were really concerned about the investigation, would have been -- just a moment -- carry out the investigation to see what happened, to collect all vestiges and remnants and then the field would be cleared. I think that's the question. Why didn't you say that during the meeting, "Before collecting the bodies, let's carry out the investigation. Let's get the proof. Let's get the evidence, the vestiges and things." That's the question.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, this was not my choice. I had to implement the order of two commanders who were my superiors. All my positions, including my requests and my orders, were given in writing to the chief of staff of the main staff, on the 24th of April, 1993. I was concerned about the investigation and the bodies were not delivered on the same moment. That's another issue, the conditions under which we worked. But this order emanates from an order that I was given by two superiors, two people who were superior to me, both the chief of staff of the main staff of the BH army and the chief of staff of the main staff of the HVO, and I gave the order for an investigation on the 24th of April, '93, and I was, indeed, keen that it should be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps before we break, could I put a question to the witness for the sake of completeness, because this is a very interesting question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the collection of the dead from Ahmici, when you did that, did you discover the number of dead, the composition, how many were elderly, women, children, civilians, or soldiers, and the method in which they were killed? Did you, by collecting those bodies, discover those data?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a report written with a detailed description and identification of the dead that could?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and an exchange on the basis of the criteria of international organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This collection carefully, with a report indicating the sex, the identity, et cetera, did this help in identifying the consequences of the crime in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Until then, we only had the data given to us by Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We had planned to come to that later, but I thought it would be better to raise that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will take a break. We will take 20 minutes because General Blaskic has had to answer a great number of questions. We'll take 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are continuing with your statement. We're talking about the 30th of April, 1993. We have completed the previous day with the order that we discussed a few minutes ago. Tell me, what were the most important events on the 30th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1993, again we had refugees coming in from Zenica to Vitez and Busovaca, and then there was the question of the meeting with Mr. Franjo Nakic and my intention to authorise him to have powers equal to mine in the joint commission in terms of adopting orders, that is to say, we were agreeing on new forms of work in the joint command. I also gave instructions to speed up the establishment of the Vitez Brigade, and I told my security assistant to cooperate with the civilian defence in order to collect all the necessary data, and then I ordered him to investigate fully up to the names and surnames of the perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying "investigation." What investigation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Investigation into the crime committed in Ahmici. Again I told him to go to the very end, that is to say, to the names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you sent an SIS officer, who was in charge of the investigation of what happened in Ahmici, to cooperate with the civilian defence. Could you please explain to the Court what you meant by this? Why the civilian defence? Why would that be related to the investigation of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the practice was that whenever the front line was being taken care of, it was never done by members of the military units but by the members of the civilian defence, that is to say, civilians who were mobilised for tasks related to the civilian defence, and then they collected corpses and, as much as possible, post-mortems were conducted by civilians. Soldiers did not take part in this and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we stopped at the point when we were discussing civilian defence units who were collecting dead bodies from the front line. Tell me, specifically in the case of Ahmici, who collected the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The members of the civilian defence of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what they ascertained, how long the list was of the persons they found in Ahmici, and did they submit this to your investigating authorities?
